summary: A US envoy carries Ukraine's ideas to Putin, Yemen's war draws in British jets, Ebola reaches Nigeria, a drone strike hits Abyei, the EU eyes the Arctic, and AI agents hack websites.

topics.heading: US envoy meets Zelenskyy in Oslo, then flies to Russia to see Putin
topics.summary: After talks in Norway that US and European officials called constructive, envoy Steve Witkoff arrived in St Petersburg to meet Vladimir Putin on Wednesday. Zelenskyy says vital US intelligence on Russian attacks has been restored.

lead.title: Witkoff in Russia for Putin meeting after 'positive' talks with Zelenskyy

alsoReported.title: US envoy Witkoff to meet Putin, Trump presses Kyiv to settle
Zelenskiy goes to Oslo for US talks as Trump tensions mount

article: On Tuesday, US envoy Steve Witkoff met Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo, with the leaders of Norway and Finland and EU and NATO officials in the room[^2]. A US official called the talks "constructive" and said they covered security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and Europe's wider security[^2]. Witkoff then flew to St Petersburg, where he is due to meet Vladimir Putin on Wednesday[^1][^4].

The meeting came as US-Ukraine relations hit a low point. Days earlier, President Donald Trump said it was "time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine" and that Zelenskyy did not want to stop the war[^3]. Kyiv had complained that Washington stopped sharing warnings of incoming Russian missiles, held up Patriot air-defence interceptors and let the military Starlink satellite service be slowed[^2]. After Oslo, Zelenskyy said the intelligence had been restored[^1][^2].

Background: the US has tried to broker a deal since 2025, but Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on territory and on who would guarantee a peace. Trump has recently lifted sanctions on Russian diesel, which he links to lowering US fuel prices before the November 3 midterms; that drew criticism from both parties in Congress[^2][^3]. Europe wants a seat at the table: the EU's foreign-policy chief said Ukraine has not surrendered "because Europe has been supporting Ukraine"[^3].

What could happen next: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Witkoff will carry Ukraine's ideas to the Russian side "and let's see if we can make some progress"[^1]. Witkoff is also expected to raise the case of Stephen Hubbard, an American held in a Russian prison[^4]. My read: watch whether the Kremlin moves on anything concrete, such as an energy truce, or only on talks about talks.
topics.differences: Kyiv says the US held back intelligence, Patriots and Starlink access; Rubio says there was no political decision to harm Ukraine and that Trump had nothing to do with Starlink's choices[^1][^2]. The Wall Street Journal and Reuters reported the Starlink slowdown involved the White House; Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth says Washington did not restrict it[^2]. Some Republican senators accuse the administration of giving in to Russia[^3].

topics.heading: Houthi missiles kill 73 Yemeni recruits as the UK sends jets to defend Saudi skies
topics.summary: Yemen's deadliest strike in months hit a training camp in Shabwa province. Britain says RAF Typhoons will patrol over Saudi Arabia, and Iran tells Pakistan's mediator there will be no talks with Washington until its conditions are met.

lead.title: Death toll rises to 73 in Houthi strike on Yemen training camp in deadliest attack in months

alsoReported.title: The UK expands military support for Saudi Arabia against Houthis to include 'defensive' air patrols
Iran's Pezeshkian discusses mediation efforts in meeting with Pakistan's army chief

article: Three ballistic missiles hit the al-Alam training camp in Yemen's Shabwa province on Monday as new recruits lined up, according to provincial authorities[^5]. By Tuesday the death toll had risen to 73, with more than 200 wounded; officials say the victims were 18 to 20 years old and were training for local security, not front-line combat[^5]. The Houthis, the Iran-aligned movement that controls much of north Yemen, claimed the attack[^5].

Yemen's war, which began in 2014, flared again in July after a 2022 truce broke down; since then the Houthis have fired missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government[^5]. On Tuesday, Saudi authorities said they intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile near Riyadh's main airport[^5].

Britain is stepping up. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said RAF Typhoon jets will fly "defensive counter-air operations" over Saudi Arabia to protect cities and infrastructure, but will not strike Houthi targets[^6]. Britain is also sending advisers and a transport plane, and extending its air-refuelling mission by 90 days[^6]. The US envoy Tom Barrack said the US would give logistical support but not troops[^5].

The wider Iran war is still stuck. Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, met Iran's president in Tehran to push mediation[^7]. Iran's parliament speaker said Washington cannot earn trust until it meets seven Iranian conditions, including lifting the US blockade of Iran's ports and sanctions on its oil[^7]. My read: the Yemen front is now the most active part of the conflict, and each new outside force, British jets now and possibly Egyptian help after next week's vote, makes it harder to contain.

topics.heading: Ebola reaches Nigeria as Kenya confirms a ninth case
topics.summary: Nigeria has its first confirmed case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, in a traveller from Uganda. Kenya's nine cases are all in one family cluster, while Congo has counted more than 9,000 cases since May.

lead.title: Nigeria confirms first Ebola case amid concerns about continental spread

alsoReported.title: Nigeria confirms first Ebola case as outbreak spreads across Africa

article: Nigeria confirmed its first Ebola case on Tuesday: a woman in the capital, Abuja, who had travelled from Uganda, fell ill on October 7 and was treated at a private hospital before being diagnosed[^8][^9]. She is in isolation, and health officials are tracing 44 people she was in close contact with[^8][^9]. Health Minister Muhammad Pate said Nigeria is doing "everything possible" to contain it[^8].

Kenya confirmed its ninth case the same day, a 24-year-old relative of its first patient, who died in Nairobi on October 5[^8]. He was already in quarantine. Kenya's health director said all nine cases belong to one cluster, with no sign of spread beyond it, and almost all 135 known contacts have been traced[^8].

Background: this outbreak began in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in May. It is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no licensed vaccine or specific treatment[^8]. Congo has recorded more than 9,000 cases and about 4,400 deaths[^8][^9]. Europe's disease agency calls it the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record[^8]. Ebola spreads through close contact with the body fluids of sick people, which is why tracing contacts matters so much.

Why it matters: Nigeria is Africa's most populous country and a travel hub for West Africa. The head of the Africa CDC called the outbreak an "extremely serious threat" and asked other countries for money, supplies and health workers[^9]. Ebola can take up to three weeks to cause symptoms. My read: the coming weeks will show whether Nigeria's case stays isolated.

topics.heading: A drone strike on a market in disputed Abyei kills scores of people
topics.summary: Local officials blame Sudan's army for Monday's strike near a fuel depot in the region claimed by both Sudan and South Sudan. Reported death tolls range from 73 to 220, and the army says it hit fuel meant for its rival, the RSF.

lead.title: South Sudan says Sudanese drone attack killed scores in Abyei market

alsoReported.title: Sudanese army says deadly Abyei drone strike targeted RSF fuel supplies

article: On Monday around midday, drones struck Amiet market in Abyei, a strip of land claimed by both Sudan and South Sudan[^10][^11]. The death toll is still uncertain. Abyei's caretaker information minister first told Reuters about 73 people were killed and 19 wounded, and later told Sudans Post the toll had reached 220 and could rise[^10][^11]. The aid group MSF said it was treating more than 20 wounded people, some with burns[^10][^11].

The minister blamed Sudan's army, without giving evidence, and South Sudan summoned Sudan's ambassador in protest[^10][^11]. A senior Sudanese army officer, speaking anonymously, said the army carried out the strike against fuel tankers supplying the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary group it has been fighting since 2023, and said "we do not target civilians"[^11]. Reuters reported that a diplomatic source said the depot had been used to supply the RSF, which it could not verify[^10]. The UN condemned the attacks, saying women and children were among the dead[^11].

Background: Abyei's status was meant to be settled by a referendum under a 2005 peace deal, but that vote never happened because the two sides disagreed on who could vote[^11]. A UN peacekeeping force is based there[^10]. Sudan's war has turned more and more to drones; Reuters cites local rights groups reporting dozens killed in other strikes this month[^10].

Why it matters: Sudan's war has created one of the world's largest humanitarian crises, and strikes in a border zone risk pulling South Sudan in. My read: whether the UN or another neutral body investigates will shape how this attack is understood.
topics.differences: Abyei officials and South Sudan blame Sudan's army and describe a market full of civilians[^10][^11]. A Sudanese army officer says the target was RSF fuel tankers and that the dead were RSF members or fuel smugglers[^11]. Death toll reports from the same Abyei official range from 73 to 220[^10][^11].

topics.heading: The EU puts security first in a new Arctic strategy, with Canada as a key partner
topics.summary: The European Commission's plan calls the Arctic a front line, citing Russian drone incursions and cable sabotage. It proposes shared icebreakers, a protected undersea cable to Greenland and closer work with Canada and Norway.

lead.title: EU revises Arctic strategy as pressure from Russia, US grows

alsoReported.title: EU's new Arctic strategy declares the region a 'front line,' eyes shared icebreakers and military rail

article: On Tuesday, the European Commission released a new Arctic strategy, replacing its 2021 policy and putting security and resilience first[^12][^13]. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the Arctic is where "the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding"[^12]. EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas pointed to Russian drone incursions, GPS jamming (blocking satellite navigation signals) and cable sabotage in the far north[^12].

The plan includes a hub for monitoring ships and protecting undersea internet cables, a secure cable from Greenland to Europe, more EU-owned satellites for government communications, and pooled buying of icebreakers, which the EU says it lacks[^12][^13]. It sets aside €200 million for Greenland in 2026 and 2027 and calls for faster rail links so military equipment can move north[^13]. On climate, it keeps the EU's position that Arctic oil, coal and gas should stay in the ground, though it drops a push for a legal ban on new drilling[^12][^13].

Canada features prominently. It is named in a new cooperation framework with Norway, Iceland, the UK, the US, Greenland and the Faroe Islands, and a planned cable to Japan and South Korea would run through Canadian waters[^13]. An EU-Canada summit is set for October 29-30[^13].

Why it matters: melting ice is opening new shipping routes and access to resources, and both Russia and the US are pressing their interests. Several measures aim to reduce Europe's dependence on Washington, after President Trump's repeated demands to control Greenland, a Danish territory[^12]. The plan now goes to EU governments and the European Parliament[^13]. My read: Canada may gain leverage as Europe looks for Arctic partners other than the US.

topics.heading: A hacker reportedly let AI agents break into more than 100 company websites
topics.summary: A security researcher told Reuters he watched AI agents, given short instructions, probe more than 1,200 sites and get into over 100, at a cost of about $5,000. Victims include sites of Deere and SharkNinja.

lead.title: A Chinese hacker used AI agents to break into more than 100 company websites

alsoReported.title: Hacker Leverages AI Agents to Breach More Than 100 Company Websites

article: Reuters reported on Monday that a Chinese-speaking hacker used AI agents, programs that can plan and carry out multi-step tasks on their own, to attack company websites in the US, Canada, Australia and Japan[^14][^15]. Snorre Fagerland, a researcher at the security firm NorForge, said he saw the activity through copies of an open-source AI platform that had been accidentally left exposed online[^14].

According to the reports, the hacker gave the agents fewer than 100 Chinese characters of instructions, and they then worked largely without supervision[^14]. They tried more than 1,200 websites and got into more than 100, with a successful break-in typically taking about 23 hours[^15]. Fagerland estimated the total cost at about $5,000 in AI usage fees[^15]. In one case, the agents searched public records, found an exposed control panel and used a weakness to run commands[^14]. Fagerland said, "It's not script kiddie stuff," meaning it was more skilled than amateur hacking[^14].

Named targets include Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins. SharkNinja said only a product-support site was affected, and Deere said it saw no sign sensitive data was accessed[^14][^15]. One hacker Fagerland watched reportedly stole credit-card data, but the full extent of theft is unknown[^14][^15]. WinBuzzer reports the tools appeared to include DeepSeek and Anthropic's Claude Code[^15]. (Anthropic also makes Claude, the AI that writes this brief.)

Why it matters: if AI makes skilled break-ins cheap and fast, many more attackers can try them, and defenders will need to patch weaknesses faster too. These findings come from one researcher's observations and have not been independently confirmed, so treat the numbers with care[^15]. My read: this is an early sign of how AI agents change cybersecurity for ordinary companies, not only for governments.

question.text: If AI agents make breaking into websites cheap enough that almost anyone can try, what might change over the next few years, not just for hackers and companies, but for the ordinary people whose data those companies hold?

read.title: A rare Ebola strain is spreading. Here's why it's so hard to contain.
read.summary: A clear explainer from May, when this outbreak began, on the Bundibugyo strain: how it spreads, why there is no vaccine yet, and why tracing contacts and safe burials are the main tools.
